title: Why Γ is not a tensor, and why that is fine
promptMarkdown: In under 200 words, and without the notes open, explain why the Christoffel symbols are not the components of a tensor although the covariant derivative is a tensor operation. Use polar coordinates on the flat plane as your example. Then say, in two sentences, what would be different about Γ in a genuinely curved space and what would be the same.
hintLadder: What are the Christoffel symbols in Cartesian coordinates on the plane? In polar coordinates? What does that tell you, given how tensors behave under coordinate changes?
Which two non-tensorial transformation terms cancel in $\partial_\beta V^\mu + \Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}V^\alpha$?

criteria.criterion: Γ vanishes in Cartesian coordinates and equals (1/r, −r) in polar coordinates on the same flat plane; a tensor zero in one chart is zero in all; hence Γ is not a tensor (its law has an inhomogeneous term).

∂_β V^μ also has an inhomogeneous term (second derivatives of the coordinate map); the two inhomogeneous terms cancel in ∇_β V^μ, which is the component form of the geometric derivative of the vector field.

In a curved space no coordinates make Γ vanish on an open set (only at a point, to first order); Γ still comes from the metric by the same formula, ∇ is still defined the same way and ∇g = 0 still holds.
